summary:
Vologda Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia, where legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023 and where the Supreme Court's designation of the "international LGBT movement" as an extremist organisation in November 2023 governs enforcement. No regional deviation specific to Vologda Oblast has been identified at the national score, so a trans visitor in the oblast faces the same legal exposure as elsewhere in the country.

Gender-marker changes on official documents are prohibited. Any identity check by police, at a hotel or on transport therefore reads as a mismatch between presentation and paperwork, with no lawful route to correct it; the mismatch persists for the whole stay and cannot be resolved by presenting a foreign document. Same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are both banned, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023.

The expanded "propaganda" statute criminalises public expression that, explicitly, justifies gender transition. Under the UK Home Office country policy and information note on Russia (SOGI, June 2025), the 2013 law carries administrative fines of up to 400,000 rubles for individuals or detention of up to 15 days, with repeated offences escalating to criminal prosecution and up to four years' imprisonment. Since the November 2023 extremist designation, participation in the designated movement carries two to six years' imprisonment and organising it six to ten years under Article 282.2.

Foreign nationals who violate these laws face arrest, detention of up to 15 days and deportation, and official national government warnings directed at LGBT travellers state this explicitly. The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings addressed to LGBT travellers.

Enforcement volume is documented. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions as of 30 June 2025, of which about 98 were administrative and three criminal, for alleged participation in the designated movement or for displaying its symbols. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges, including three publishing-house staff charged in May 2025 under Article 282.2 who each face up to 12 years' imprisonment, while 81 people were found guilty in 98 administrative cases under Article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols.

The UK Home Office assesses that openly LGBT+ people in Russia are likely to face discriminatory treatment that, by its nature or repetition, may amount to persecution, with the state able but not willing to provide protection, and records at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024. The same note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.
tangentialFactors:
The post-designation crackdown moved quickly. The Guardian reported on 17 January 2024 that within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night. The Moscow Times reported on 23 June 2025 that arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, quoting a St Petersburg queer woman who described herself as "a second-class citizen" after the extremist designation.

Enforcement is escalating in scale as well as severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility. Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented alongside the legal regime. BBC Russian followed "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found. The case illustrates a national pattern rather than anything specific to Vologda Oblast.
localsOnly:
Residents of Vologda Oblast live under the same prohibitions as visitors, but with no possibility of departure as a remedy. Gender-affirming care was banned in 2023, legal gender recognition is unavailable, and gender-marker changes on Russian documents are prohibited, so residents carry the presentation-paperwork mismatch indefinitely with no lawful route to correct it.

Same-sex marriage is banned for residents, and same-sex sexual activity is not itself criminalised. Public expression justifying gender transition exposes residents to administrative fines of up to 400,000 rubles or detention of up to 15 days, rising to criminal prosecution and up to four years on repetition.

Participation in the designated extremist movement carries two to six years' imprisonment and organising it six to ten years under Article 282.2, and displaying its symbols is prosecuted under Article 20.3. The 139 people recorded by the UK Home Office as impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024 are Russian residents, not travellers.
outOfScopeNotes:
No enforcement data specific to Vologda Oblast has been sourced: the oblast is scored at the national level because no regional deviation was identified, and the conviction and case figures cited here are national totals reported by Human Rights Watch and the UK Home Office rather than counts from Vologda courts or police.

The record does not resolve how often identity documents are checked in practice within Vologda Oblast, whether local police or hotel staff apply the document mismatch rule, or whether any local medical or support services exist in the oblast for trans visitors. The conversion-therapy case in the source material concerns a centre near Novosibirsk and is not evidence of comparable facilities in Vologda Oblast. Regional variation in the pace of extremism charges across Russian oblasts remains not sourced.
